A.explanation: Starts with upward velocity of opposite sign to the final downward velocity, but it is a straight line of constant gradient. Constant gradient means constant acceleration $g$ with no air resistance.

B.explanation: Starts with upward velocity, crosses zero at the top, then shows increasing downward velocity with decreasing gradient as air resistance grows toward terminal velocity.

C.explanation: Shows the stone starting upward and returning to zero velocity at impact. The stone hits the sea with large downward velocity, not zero.

D.explanation: Shows the speed increasing with increasing gradient after the top and does not keep the correct sign change. With air resistance the magnitude of acceleration must decrease, not increase.

hints: Notice the stone is thrown vertically upwards but hits the sea moving downwards, so on a velocity-time graph the line must start on one side of the time axis and finish on the opposite side.
Remember the gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration, and air resistance always opposes the velocity so the resultant force and acceleration are reduced below $mg$ divided by mass.
Compare the long downward fall to the sea: with growing drag the net acceleration shrinks, so the graph must curve to a smaller gradient rather than stay straight.
walkthrough: Take upward as negative and downward as positive, as in graphs A and B. The stone is released with upward velocity, so the graph must start below the time axis with $v < 0$, and must end above the axis with large $v > 0$ when it hits the sea.

On the way up, weight acts down and drag acts down, so deceleration is greater than $g$. As the stone slows, drag falls, so the magnitude of deceleration falls and the $v$-$t$ gradient magnitude gets smaller.
At the top $v = 0$ where the graph crosses the time axis. After that the stone falls down, so $v > 0$ and both speed and upward drag increase.

On the way down, weight acts down and drag acts up, so net downward acceleration is $a = g - F_{drag}/m$. As speed rises, $F_{drag}$ rises and $a$ falls, so the gradient of the $v$-$t$ graph must decrease.
With the long drop from the cliff to the sea the curve flattens toward constant terminal velocity, not a straight line of constant $g$. Graph A is straight and ignores air resistance.
Only the curve that starts negative, crosses zero once, then rises with ever-decreasing positive gradient matches this. This is option B.
